prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling frequency measurement at the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock (B048) as a sole prize part for Katori and Ye. After the full first-round exchange the case has not weakened. Every member ranked it in the top three, and six of eight prefer it, but what persuades me is that the supporters' arguments are independent of each other and survive each other's objections: the magic-wavelength lattice removes the dominant trapping light shift so that many neutral atoms can be interrogated at once; this is a different concept from the single-ion control honoured in 2012; uncertainties near 1e-18 have been reproduced and intercompared in several laboratories; and the consequences (preparation for redefining the second, relativistic geodesy, limits on varying constants and dark-sector couplings) are concrete. The two-name credit maps onto concept and first strontium realisation (Katori) and record accuracy and many-body regimes (Ye). My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1. I have not moved toward any other configuration, and I am not adding a second part, because I see no second candidate whose maturity and clean attribution match the clock.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 prize (frequency comb, Hall and Haensch) and the 2012 prize (control of single quantum systems, Wineland) is real, and the citation has to be worded so that it honours the lattice-clock invention and does not read as a general prize for optical clocks. Other groups (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom, the Paris and PTB efforts) are outside the credited names, so two names are a judgment on credit and not a partition of it. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so part of the fundamental-physics payoff is still prospective. My views on the Katori and Ye division of credit rest on general knowledge and not on documents in this record.

responses.point: You say the 2025 prize should weigh more heavily against circuit QED (B001), that Devoret and Girvin outside the credited trio make that set a compromise, and you ask how I weigh the proximity argument.
responses.response: I agree with your timeliness and attribution points, and I have dropped B001 as a preferred option. On proximity: I direct WACQT and work in circuit and waveguide QED, so I am an interested party for B001 and should not lead on it. I would not advocate it in this round, and I think my view should be discounted wherever it favours circuit QED. Separately, I accept your argument that the demonstrated impact of the clock outweighs the timing argument for waiting, because a citation can describe the invention and development without depending on the formal redefinition.

responses.point: You ask whether a second part, for example trapped-ion quantum logic (B003), should share the prize with B048, and you note the credit boundary with the comb and the Hall laboratory.
responses.response: I do not favour adding B003 now. Cirac and Zoller are outstanding theory, but the 2012 prize already recognised control of single quantum systems and Monroe and other ion groups have experimental claims that Blatt alone does not cover. A trio on B003 would also use all three names and force a split with B048 that would leave no room to correct the clock credit if the committee wants a third name later. I keep B003 as an alternative. I also take your point that your time in Hall's laboratory is a field proximity to the comb prize, but it does not bear on the credited names, and I would not treat it as a reason for recusal.

responses.point: You prefer B019 for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, as a prediction confirmed by experiment with nearly two decades of independent confirmation, and you note that the 2016 topology prize and the prospective technology weigh against it.
responses.response: I take your confirmation argument seriously and B019 remains my first alternative. My remaining difficulty is the one you state yourself: the credited trio omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe proposal pointed Molenkamp to the material, and the three-dimensional work of Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents. With a three-name limit, the citation would have to describe the HgTe observation in a way that the omitted prediction makes hard to defend. I would revisit B019 if the committee finds a credit configuration that handles the HgTe prediction, but that is not available within the supplied names.

responses.point: You note that broad support does not by itself make B048 the best choice, that nobody's favourite is strongly contested, and that you see no natural fit for a two-part prize with a one-person part.
responses.response: I agree that breadth of ranking is not a merit argument, and I have tried to rest my case on the physics. The right test is whether B048 survives the objections made in round 1, and I think it does: the Stark-shift argument separates it from single-ion clocks, and independent 1e-18 results address maturity. I also agree about the two-part question: no shortlisted second part fits cleanly alongside two clock laureates, and adding one only for the sake of a larger prize would be the artificial consensus the protocol warns against.

responses.point: You prefer B028 (spherical-aberration correction in TEM) but say that B048 would be a defensible outcome, and you flag that Krivanek and STEM correction work are omitted.
responses.response: Your case is concrete and I respect that you offer it as an outlier view. My concern is the same one you name: a TEM-only trio for Rose, Haider and Urban settles a priority question against Krivanek and the STEM work, and it follows the 1986 microscopy prize. I do not think I should rank instrument-enabling work against the clock on a field I do not know, but the clock also enables measurement and I think it does so with a clearer chain from concept to a result used by other fields. I appreciate that you do not see a conflict for B048, and I see none for B028 either.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 single-quantum-system prize as a real obstacle to a lattice-clock prize, or accepts that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct invention.

Whether two names fairly cover the lattice clock given Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom and the Paris and PTB groups, and whether my Katori and Ye division of credit would survive verification against the primary papers.
Whether acting before the formal redefinition of the second is right; I judge it is, but I cannot rule out that waiting would give a better-framed citation.
Whether my closeness to superconducting-circuit physics has biased me, in either direction, in my reading of the 2025 prize and of B001.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I am a circuit and waveguide QED theorist and director of WACQT at Chalmers, with documented connections to Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum; Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. I would recuse myself from any discussion that makes B001 (circuit QED) the lead, and I do not advocate it. My profile shows no specific connection to Katori or Ye, nor to the credited names of B019 or B003, so none is apparent for my preferred configuration or alternatives.
